papers.title: Reducing Risk Through Trade Credit: Theory and Evidence from Dual-Channel Suppliers
papers.abstract: Trade credit is traditionally viewed as increasing supplier risk, because delayed payments expose suppliers to buyer uncertainties. Using a stylized game-theoretic model, we show that this conventional wisdom can be overturned when a supplier is dual channel: operating a direct channel that sells to end customers in addition to an indirect channel that sells to an industry peer who serves the same market. Compared with zero trade credit provision where the supplier requires cash on delivery (COD), we observe empirically that high trade credit provision can lead to lower risk for the dual-channel supplier. We propose a possible mechanism for this risk mitigation effect—pooling: When the market overlap between the supplier and its peer buyer is sufficiently high, the random split of the overlapping market creates negative association between the supplier’s direct channel sales and the buyer’s trade credit payment. Trade credit does not always mitigate risk for dual-channel suppliers. If the supplier’s debt level is high, our theory predicts that trade credit exacerbates risk. We find empirical evidence consistent with our theoretical predictions using data on U.S. manufacturing firms that sell to their industry peers. The positive association between trade credit provision and bankruptcy risk is dampened or even reversed once a supplier begins selling to peer firms. papers.title: Inferential Theory for Pricing Errors with Latent Factors and Firm Characteristics
papers.abstract: We study factor models that combine latent factors with firm characteristics and propose a new framework for modeling, estimating, and inferring pricing errors. Following Zhang (2024), our approach decomposes mispricing into two distinct components: inside alpha, explained by firm characteristics but orthogonal to factor exposures, and outside alpha, orthogonal to both factors and characteristics. Our model generalizes those developed recently such as Kelly et al. (2019) and Zhang (2024), resolving issues of orthogonality, basis dependence, and unit sensitivity. Methodologically, we develop estimators grounded in low-rank methods with explicit debiasing, providing closed-form solutions and a rigorous inferential theory that accommodates a growing number of characteristics and relaxes standard assumptions on sample dimensions. Empirically, using U.S. stock returns from 2000 to 2019, we document strong evidence of both inside and outside alphas, with the former showing industry-level comovements and the latter reflecting idiosyncratic shocks beyond firm fundamentals. Our framework thus unifies statistical and characteristic-based approaches to factor modeling, offering both theoretical advances and new insights into the structure of pricing errors. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This research was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grant DMS-2052955]. papers.title: Echoes of Discord: The Effects of Global Conflicts and Disputes on Entrepreneurship
papers.abstract: Mixed-nationality founding teams bring together heterogeneous, hard-to-replicate bundles of human capital and country-specific ties through their cross-national networks, providing a distinctive foundation for building successful ventures. Yet these connections may be vulnerable to nonmarket shocks. This study examines whether geopolitical conflicts and disputes between the countries of origin of immigrant founders affect the formation of new ventures. Leveraging data on the founders of start-ups established in Great Britain and global information on conflicts and disputes, I find that such tensions reduce the likelihood that nationals of hostile countries cofound firms together. The evidence is more consistent with social mechanisms and, particularly, the erosion of interpersonal relationships than with diminished access to cross-country resources or the loss of entrepreneurial opportunities. Start-ups of both low and high quality are affected, including in sectors that depend heavily on skilled human capital, such as high-tech and business services. The negative effect is substantially attenuated for nationality pairs that are heavily colocated across local areas and for founders with prior social exposure to individuals from the opposing nationality, indicating that interpersonal ties can buffer against geopolitical shocks. Conflicts do not affect the exit of existing firms, and the decline in mixed-nationality entrepreneurship is not offset by alternative team …

papers.title: Correcting the Unobserved Textual Confounding Factors in Regression by BERT and Partially Linear Regression
papers.abstract: In the last decade, there has been a surge of text-mining applications in the information systems literature. In these applications, researchers typically construct independent variables from documents by various text-mining techniques. The most prominent example could be using online review sentiments to investigate online word-of-mouth issues. Typically, most documents contain information richer than the independent variable, and researchers may construct control variables from the same documents to alleviate endogeneity issues. However, researchers need to manually craft these variables, and this process may not guarantee that all the important confounding factors are extracted and included in the regression model with a correct functional form. If useful textual information is overlooked and a valid identification strategy is not available, the omitted variable bias may occur. To solve this challenge, we propose a novel model that utilizes text embedding based on the state-of-the-art neural network language model (i.e., bidirectional encoder representations from transformers (BERT)) to automatically create a new control variable vector for controlling latent confounding factors in the absence of a valid identification strategy. Moreover, our approach can be considered a semiparametric approach in that our model contains a linear term of the key independent variable and an unknown functional term of the textual control variables. Our approach extends the semiparametric …

papers.title: Online Allocation of Throughput-Constrained Resources Using Proxy Assignments
papers.abstract: Problem definition: We study a variation of the canonical online resource allocation problem in which resources are throughput, rather than budget, constrained. As in the classical setting, the decision-maker must assign sequentially arriving jobs to one of multiple available resources. However, in addition to the assignment costs incurred from these decisions, the decision-maker is also penalized for deviating from exogenous, time-varying target assignment rates for each resource, which represent the resources’ respective throughput capacities throughout the horizon. The goal is to minimize the total expected assignment and deviation penalty costs incurred throughout the horizon when the distribution of assignment costs is unknown. Methodology/results: We first show that naive extensions of state-of-the-art algorithms for classical budget-constrained resource allocation problems can fail dramatically when applied to throughput-constrained resource allocation. We then propose a novel “proxy assignment“ primal-dual algorithm that uses current arrivals to simulate the effect of future arrivals. We prove that our algorithm achieves the optimal $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound when the assignment costs of the arriving jobs are drawn i.i.d. from a fixed distribution. We demonstrate the practical performance of our approach by conducting numerical experiments on synthetic datasets, as well as real-world datasets from retail fulfillment operations. papers.title: Tax-induced Corporate In-kind Donations: Equilibrium Analysis and Policy Design
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Food-sector firms often make in-kind donations to help alleviate food insecurity. For example, major retailers such as Walmart and Kroger routinely donate products to food banks. To encourage such donations, many governments offer tax incentives to donor firms. We examine how tax incentives affect firms’ operational and donation decisions, profits and consumer surplus, and we investigate the optimal design of such incentives. Methodology/results: We develop an analytical model to study a firm’s operational and in-kind donation decisions under capacity constraints, in a setting where consumers with heterogeneous valuations can either purchase a product from the firm or attempt to obtain a donated product from charitable organizations. Among other findings, we identify a threshold of the tax incentive rate above which the firm is willing to donate. While the firm always benefits from more generous incentives, consumer surplus follows a U-shaped relationship with respect to the incentive rate: a moderate incentive may result in lower consumer surplus than no incentive at all. Further, the optimal tax policy depends on the government’s emphasis on social welfare, with donation tax incentives becoming desirable only when sufficient weight is placed on social welfare. These findings remain robust when accounting for competition from fringe firms and consumer heterogeneity in the acceptance of donated products. Finally, as an alternative policy intervention, …

papers.title: Embedded in Two Worlds: How Incumbents’ Brokerage Affects Adaptation When Old and New Supply Networks Coexist
papers.abstract: The development of new technology architectures often opens up new markets within an existing industry. Incumbents face the decision of whether to enter the new technology market and how to do so. As incumbents attempt to enter the new market, they can become embedded in two buyer-supplier networks, one for the old and the other for new technologies. We argue that brokers have an advantage in this process because they have developed capabilities to integrate suppliers of new technology components or develop unique component combinations for the new technology products. In a study of the U.S. automotive industry between 2012 and 2022, we find that brokerage in the old technology network is positively associated with successful entry into the new technology (i.e., number and performance of new technology models). Surprisingly, brokerage in the old technology network had a stronger positive impact than brokerage in the new technology network on incumbents’ entry into the new technology market for electric vehicles.

papers.title: Democratic Organizing and Contemporary Managerial Talent Markets: Internal Promotion or External Hiring?
papers.abstract: We develop and empirically examine a theoretical framework explaining the relationship between democratic organizing and firms’ propensity to staff management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. Conventionally, the advantages of promoting through internal labor markets (ILM) have rested on the assumption that workers value intra-firm careers and anticipate remaining with the same employer for a longer term. These advantages may prove harder to attain in contemporary labor markets, given that declining tenure and workers’ growing preference for inter-firm careers possibly reduce the information advantage of ILM and undermine internal candidate retention. We propose that firms with more democratic organizing are less susceptible to these ILM challenges, enjoy higher benefits from recruiting internally and are thus more likely to fill management positions through internal promotion. Using longitudinal employer-employee linked data for Danish firms from 2001 to 2017, we find that firms with worker board representation (WBR), one form of more democratic organizing, are more likely than firms without WBR to fill management positions through internal promotion rather than external hiring. This association is stronger where (i) worker representatives have broader intra-firm experience and are more likely to possess promotion-relevant information; (ii) more managers and professionals have peers serving as worker representatives on the board. papers.title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence from a University Debating Competition
papers.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) and work reports both productivity-compressing and inequality-expanding effects, leaving open a central question for organizations: Who benefits from GenAI and on which specific tasks? I address this question through a randomized controlled trial in competitive university debating, where participants are randomly assigned access to GenAI. Although most previous experimental work examines the impact of GenAI on written activities and across individuals, this setting allows me to study the impact of GenAI on a knowledge-intensive spoken activity and to identify heterogeneous effects across subtasks. I find that GenAI expands performance inequality in this setting. Consistent with recent theories on GenAI and work, results show that high-ability participants experience significantly larger gains from GenAI usage than their lower-ability counterparts in judgment-intensive subtasks, whereas lower-ability individuals only improve their performance in less expert components of debating, where GenAI can be used as a substitute. If these inequality-expanding effects generalize to similar spoken settings where complex ideas must be internalized and explained, rather than simply written, they would have important implications for understanding the impact of GenAI on work and inequality. papers.title: Scalable Just-in-Time Price Elasticity Estimation
papers.abstract: This paper presents a scalable, nonparametric approach to estimating point-wise price elasticities designed for real-time pricing decisions. A key challenge in these settings is correcting for price endogeneity while remaining computationally efficient. We address this by leveraging nonparametric control functions to decompose the identification of causal elasticities into a sequence of scalable intermediate prediction tasks. We implement this framework with bootstrap averaged (bagged) nearest neighbors, which admits a closed-form representation that enables scalable, real-time implementation. We establish uniform consistency of our estimator and show in Monte Carlo simulations that it robustly recovers local elasticities across a diverse range of data-generating processes. We demonstrate the method’s practical usefulness by applying it to the New York City ride-sharing market, recovering substantial spatial-temporal heterogeneity in price elasticity and updating citywide elasticity estimates in less than one minute, which provide a “just-in-time” input for algorithmic pricing systems. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. Funding: J. Wang acknowledges financial support from the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Grant 14508924]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04791 .

papers.title: Machine Learning Vast Dynamic Conditional Covariance Matrices: The Spirit of “Divide and Conquer”
papers.abstract: Large-scale portfolio selection requires accurate forecasts of high-dimensional dynamic conditional covariance matrices (CCMs). This task is challenging because the number of covariance elements grows quickly with the number of assets, whereas the available time-series observations are limited and noisy. In this paper, we propose a novel graph-based quantiled (GRAND) CCM estimator in the spirit of “divide and conquer.” By extracting information from the extensive asset features, the GRAND method leverages a new graph-based deep learning network, called the self-grouping autoencoder (SGA), to learn the conditional quantiles of returns. Using those learned conditional quantiles, the GRAND method further learns (co)variances of CCM element-wisely via the quantiled conditional moment (QCM) method, and finally, it makes the resulting assembled CCM estimator positive semidefinite through a projection. Because of the use of the SGA network and the QCM method in an element-wise way, the GRAND method is blessing dimensionality in learning the CCM of a large-scale portfolio, while keeping the computation manageable and maintaining causal semantics. From an extensive empirical analysis of the Chinese stock market, we show that the GRAND method can produce much better tangency portfolios than its competitors, and provide dynamic causal graphs to study variance and quantile connectedness of all stocks for interpreting systemic risk and forecasting the business cycle. papers.title: Understanding the Prompting Effects of Chain-of-Thought on Human Collaboration with Generative AI
papers.abstract: It is well established that Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning improves model performance in Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). Far less understood is whether presenting CoT reasoning in AI-enabled interfaces enhances users’ perceived trust in GenAI’s competence in performing tasks. Drawing on the Heuristic-Systematic Model, we develop a theoretical framework in which CoT presence and quality trigger either heuristic perceptions of transparency or systematic perceptions of diagnosticity and germane cognitive load, with distinct mechanisms across task-difficulty conditions. Across a series of online experiments, we identify two key findings. First, high-quality CoT consistently enhances perceived trust in GenAI’s ability to generate correct outputs, regardless of task difficulty. Notably, under high-difficulty conditions, users’ trust in GenAI is primarily driven by the greater germane cognitive load perceived from high-quality CoT, whereas under low-difficulty conditions, trust is primarily driven by perceived transparency or diagnosticity. Second, low-quality CoT reduces users’ competence trust in GenAI that generates incorrect outputs only under low-difficulty conditions and only when users engage in careful processing, operating through perceived diagnosticity. Yet, under high-difficulty conditions, low-quality CoT amplifies trust via perceived transparency. By disentangling the cognitive pathways through which CoT shapes competence trust in GenAI and by …

papers.title: When More is Better (or Not): Cybersecurity Investment, Financial Risk, and Board-Experience Heterogeneity
papers.abstract: As cybersecurity threats intensify, firm financial risk continues to rise despite growing cybersecurity investments, raising doubts about their effectiveness. We address this paradox by developing a signaling-based theoretical framework, integrating signaling theory with homophily, to explain how cybersecurity investments may relate to firm financial risk through the lens of corporate governance. Leveraging a comprehensive panel dataset from 1,071 firms over 10 years, we provide empirical evidence of a striking inverted U-shaped relationship: initial cybersecurity investments are associated with higher financial risk, but risk declines at higher levels of investment, underscoring the importance of investment scale and maturity. Board experience heterogeneity flattens this curve, dampening the rise in risk at lower levels of investment while slowing the decline at higher levels. These findings reconcile competing views of cybersecurity investment, highlight the strategic importance of board composition, and underscore the need to integrate cybersecurity investments into enterprise risk management.

papers.title: From Mining to Meaning: How Do Blockchain Infrastructure Platforms Respond to Environmental Sustainability Concerns?
papers.abstract: Environmental sustainability is a critical concern in information technology infrastructure governance, yet its implications for blockchain infrastructure platforms (BIPs), such as Bitcoin, largely fall outside the regulatory mechanisms that govern centralized firms. This study exploits Tesla’s suspension of Bitcoin payments due to its negative environmental impact as a shock to investor awareness of BIPs’ environmental impacts. Consistent with nonpecuniary preference theory in behavioral finance, we find that BIPs, especially energy-intensive proof-of-work-based platforms, experience losses in token valuations following the suspension. We further find that, after the suspension, investors value environmental disclosures more positively, and BIPs substantially increase environmental disclosures. Our findings highlight investor awareness as a market-based governance mechanism for mitigating blockchain infrastructures’ environmental impacts.

papers.title: Governing Value Creation on Livestreaming Platforms: Intervention, Privilege Structure, and Streamer Adaptation
papers.abstract: Platform governance shapes not only how value is created in digital ecosystems but also who is better positioned to create it. Yet little is known about how governance interventions triggered by external pressures affect value creation across platform privilege structures. We investigate a bitrate restriction on Twitch, a global livestreaming platform, in South Korea. Implemented in response to rising network fees, this governance intervention constrained streamers’ access to a critical operational resource. We find that the intervention reduced streamer value creation, measured by average concurrent viewership, by approximately 9.6%. This harm was unevenly distributed, concentrating among the least-privileged streamers, while more-privileged streamers appeared partially buffered by platform-endowed technical resources and their established audience bases. Streamers reconfigured their content portfolios in response, but the performance implications of this adaptation depend on its form and platform privilege. We theorize and empirically show how resource-restricting governance interventions produce governance-induced digital inequality and condition participant adaptation in platform ecosystems.

papers.title: Knowing is Not Enough: Information Retrievability as a Precondition to Effective LLM Oversight
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded in organizational work, yet their errors often pass human review. Prior research locates such failures in users’ capability to review LLM output or their engagement in doing so. We develop an alternative, retrieval-based account of human oversight and posit that error detection is more effective when oversight-relevant information is accessible to users at the moment of review. Across two randomized lab-in-the-field experiments with 640 customer-facing employees, we show that self-generated explanations improve error detection and strengthen recall of verification-relevant reasoning, while cues that reactivate such reasoning help sustain detection under repeated LLM use. Theoretically, we identify information retrievability as a distinct precondition for effective oversight and specify generative encoding and cue-supported reactivation as mechanisms that build and sustain it. Practically, lightweight onboarding self-explanations and daily retrieval cues can make human oversight more resilient as LLM use becomes routine.

papers.title: Regulating Data Use in Social Media: Strategic Implications for Platforms and Users
papers.abstract: Social media platforms rely heavily on harvesting users’ personal data to fuel personalized engagement and maximize profits. While enhancing user engagement, this raises concerns about behavioral exploitation and user well-being, including social media addiction. In response, policymakers are considering purpose-limiting regulations on data use that restrict how platforms may use collected data, for example, by banning manipulative personalization, consistent with global initiatives such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the Digital Services Act (DSA). This paper develops a game-theoretic model to examine how such purpose-limiting regulation on data use affects platform strategies, market outcomes, and user welfare. We find that, in equilibrium, imposing this regulation may sometimes increase the amount of data collected per user, suggesting potential unintended consequences. It may also increase platform demand and profitability, and expand the market coverage while consistently enhancing overall user welfare. These findings offer theoretical and policy insights regarding regulatory impacts.

papers.title: Identifying Protected Health Information in Online Hacker Communities: A Multi-Task Relation Learning Approach
papers.abstract: Encrypted messaging platforms (e.g. Telegram and Discord) have become increasingly utilized by malicious hacker communities for the procurement and sale of stolen Protected Health Information (PHI). However, discussions posted on these platforms often contain substantial irrelevant text, making it difficult to identify and analyze such content. In this research, we propose a novel framework, PHI Named Entity Extreme Text Classification (PHI-NEXT), to address this challenge. The framework incorporates extreme text classification, named entity recognition, and multi-task relation learning to automatically identify, extract, and analyze stolen health information within encrypted messaging platforms. Results from benchmark experiments suggest that our framework significantly outperforms existing methods in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score. We further demonstrate its potential value with a case study that illustrates how cybersecurity professionals can identify emerging trends in these communities. Our study provides practical value to the cybersecurity community by presenting a design that automates the identification and analysis of stolen health information. We also contribute to the information systems knowledge base through a nascent design theory for analyzing large volumes of user-generated text.

papers.title: Still Working Late? After-Hours Mobile Technology Use, Support at Home, and Next-Day Outcomes
papers.abstract: While acknowledging the benefits of anytime-anywhere connectivity, recent research has shown that the pervasiveness of mobile technologies makes work-family conflict increasingly difficult to avoid, calling for a deeper understanding of the unintended consequences of after-hours mobile technology use for work purposes. Drawing on two complementary studies involving experience sampling methodology (ESM) and lagged survey data from working professionals, we examine how after-hours work-related mobile technology use affects employees’ recovery and subsequent work and family outcomes, as well as the conditions under which these effects can be mitigated. Our findings show that after-hours mobile technology use undermines employees’ recovery, which in turn reduces next-day concentration at work and increases spouse undermining. We also find that providing emotional support to family members buffers the negative impact of after-hours mobile technology use on recovery. Furthermore, by distinguishing among different communication channels, we show that work-related phone calls—but not emails or chats—are primarily responsible for these detrimental effects. Our findings advance Information Systems (IS) research on the work-family interface by identifying recovery as the central mechanism through which after-hours mobile technology use produces cross-domain behavioral consequences and by demonstrating that phone calls are particularly detrimental. papers.title: Impact of Problem Specification Structuredness on Crowdsourcing Contests
papers.abstract: This study explores the impacts of the structure of problem specifications in crowdsourcing contests. We theorize that the structure affects seekers’ difficulty in initiating contests, influencing the number of contests they launch. It also shapes solvers’ participation and idea generation, affecting the number of solvers and the number of high-quality ideas in contests. Using a natural experiment in which a platform increased the structuredness of problem specifications for certain contests, we find that this change led to more contests being launched by seekers. However, even with an increase in contests, individual solvers participated in fewer contests, and those contests attracted fewer solvers. Additionally, although more structured problem specifications helped individual solvers generate more high-quality submissions, there were fewer such submissions in contests. Therefore, more structured problem specifications can be a double-edged sword, making the process easier for seekers but discouraging solver participation and hindering seekers’ ability to source exceptional ideas.

papers.title: Governance as a Contingency in Cybersecurity: When Leadership Networks Help or Hurt
papers.abstract: We examine how leaders’—executives’ and directors’— social connectedness to previously breached firms shapes cybersecurity outcomes via professional and educational ties, and how corporate governance conditions its effects. We theorize a double‑edged, governance‑contingent role for these networks: they can enable intelligence transfer or foster vulnerability diffusion. Using the willingness-opportunity-ability (WOA) framework, we focus on three governance splitters: board independence (willingness to challenge), meeting frequency (opportunity to act), and leadership information technology (IT) experience (ability to interpret and implement). Leveraging breach disclosures from 2005-2024 and cumulative abnormal return (CAR) around announcements, we document sign reversals conditional on governance. Connectedness is associated with a lower breach likelihood when boards are more independent, meet more frequently, or have greater IT‑related expertise among leaders—and with a higher likelihood when these features are weak. At announcement, connectedness is associated with less negative CAR under strong governance and more negative CAR under weak governance. Thus, governance determines whether leaders’ ties yield cybersecurity resilience or vulnerability. Theoretically, this study extends social network theory to cybersecurity governance by reconceptualizing leaders’ social connectedness as a double-edged governance-contingent mechanism, and by integrating the WOA framework to …

papers.title: Too Much of a Good Thing? The Negative Impact of High-Performing Artificial Intelligence Teammates on Human Performance
papers.abstract: This study investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) teammate performance affects individual human performance in creative collaboration. Through three consecutive experiments, we find that a high-performing AI teammate paradoxically diminishes human performance through a trust-loafing pathway: members develop greater trust in the high-performing AI teammate, fostering social loafing and reducing effort. A high-performing human teammate does not trigger loafing; instead, it may activate upward social comparison, motivating individuals to match their colleague’s contributions. Additionally, a high-performing AI teammate reduces productivity disparities between high- and low-knowledge members, which occurs through high-knowledge members decreasing performance, not low-knowledge members improving. These individual-level effects transmit to the team level: teams with a high-performing AI teammate produce fewer good ideas. Theoretically, we demonstrate that AI and human teammates evoke fundamentally different social-cognitive responses, challenging the assumption that AI functions as an equivalent social actor. For practice, the results offer design recommendations, including performance-calibrated deployment and expertise-sensitive role assignment, to mitigate social loafing in human-AI teams.

papers.title: How the digital divide self-perpetuates: microbusinesses’ digital capability and their capacity to benefit from municipal initiatives fostering digital transformation
papers.abstract: Digital transformation is essential to business competitiveness, yet microbusinesses, which make up the vast majority of firms, continue to lag behind. This gap persists despite governmental initiatives to support microbusinesses’ digitalization. In this study, we build on absorptive capacity theory to propose that their effectiveness depends not only on their governance-level design but also on microbusinesses’ micro-level capacity to absorb support provided. We theorize that this capacity is driven by microbusinesses’ digital capability, i.e. the extent of their pre‑existing adoption of digital technologies, as well as their knowledge and practices regarding using them. We test our Capability-Conditioned Enablement theory in structured, in-person interviews with 100 microbusinesses (≤5 employees) in Tel Aviv, measuring firms’ digital capability using the EU’s Digital Intensity Index (DII). We show that low-digital-capability microbusinesses face disadvantages across three dimensions of digital transformation: motivation (willingness to advance digital capability); behavior (access to digital services); and evaluation of the municipality’s role in fostering digital transformation. Consequently, lower-capability firms are less likely to benefit from public digital resources, further widening the gap in comparison to higher-digital capability businesses. This study contributes a structured approach to understanding microbusinesses’ digitalization and provides actionable …

papers.title: Information Design with Supplemental Investment
papers.abstract: This paper features a setting with two-dimensional information asymmetry on a firm’s fundamental (good or bad type) and the nature of its supplemental investment (improving upside potential, or mitigating downside risk). We examine the firm’s optimal design of the information system when the system can only address the dimension of fundamental. We show that, with only single-dimensional information asymmetry regarding the firm’s fundamental, greater informativeness on the firm’s fundamental type always improves efficiency. However, with two-dimensional information asymmetry, increasing informativeness about firm fundamental no longer guarantees higher efficiency and can be detrimental. The optimal information system trades off reducing information asymmetry and preserving firms’ incentives to invest, and it could be uninformative or optimistically biased, depending on the level of credit risk, which in our setting is higher when supplemental investment is more likely to improve upside rather than protect downside. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00524 .

papers.title: Learning from a Biased Sample
papers.abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target. papers.title: Stockouts and the Success of New Products
papers.abstract: We investigate how stockouts of existing products influence the success of new product introductions. Our findings reveal that stockouts on incumbent items at the time a new product is launched are associated with higher sales of the new product for at least six months. This positive spillover is specific to new products and is most potent at the start of the product life cycle. To establish causality, we use instrumental variables based on historical stockouts and contemporaneous stockouts in other stores. Analysis of individual-level transaction data corroborates a trial-and-adoption mechanism: Stockouts of existing items prompt consumers to trial the new product, leading to increased repeat purchasing. By identifying inventory as a driver of product trial, this research highlights the importance of strategically timing new product launches and documents a previously unrecognized tradeoff for inventory policies. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02602 .

papers.title: Deep Tangency Portfolio
papers.abstract: We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. This paper was accepted by Agostino Capponi, finance. Funding: G. papers.title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
papers.abstract: The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, …

papers.title: Gatekeepers and Kingmakers: Do Superplatforms Distort Digital Competition?
papers.abstract: The rising dominance of superplatforms raises concerns about conflicts of interest and externalities on innovation, because they act as both marketplace gatekeepers and strategic investors. Studying Google’s dual role via Google Ventures (GV) and the Android marketplace, we find Google-backed startups receive 115% more reviews, 12% higher ratings, and 77% fewer bug complaints than their iOS counterparts—despite no major app updates. These gains are consistent with selective review removal and platform promotion. Using a difference-in-differences approach with iOS versions as controls, we isolate treatment from selection effects. Our findings challenge platform neutrality and highlight subtle mechanisms of competitive distortion. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The Online Appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03354 .

papers.title: Inventory Productivity and Carbon Emissions in Retailing
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Higher inventory productivity is thought to be associated with lower carbon emissions and waste. We test this conventional wisdom using granular emissions data from CDP. Methodology/results: Pairing emissions data with firms’ financials, we show that most of the emission reduction benefits emerge organically with the scale of operations. Using causal inference techniques, we show that, absent the scale, an external shock to inventory productivity results in higher emission intensity in aggregate across scopes, in Scope 3, and its category of purchased goods and services. The effect on Scope 2 emissions is negative and null in Scope 1. The effect is concentrated in the non-essential retail segments, excluding food and beverage, and health and personal care retailers. Managerial implications: All else kept equal, a higher inventory productivity trades off associated profitability benefits with upstream carbon emissions, particularly in the Scope 3 category of purchased goods and services, underscoring the need for holistic implementation of lean practices. We explore the feasibility of carbon pricing as a mechanism to shift the retailers’ calculus to the dual objective of profit maximization and minimization of environmental impact.

papers.title: How Not to Overpackage: AI for Sustainability in HelloFresh’s Service Supply Chain
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Packaging waste is a common challenge faced by meal-kit subscription services. Before shipping each box, providers must decide how much and what type of insulated packaging to use. While these materials are essential for preserving product quality, excessive use increases material waste and carbon emissions. As the industry leader, HelloFresh is committed to improving the environmental sustainability of its supply chain. Methodology/results: This paper introduces the Contextual Packaging problem and develops an online-learning method that leverages the problem structure to efficiently mitigate overpackaging. Our algorithm, Contextual Frontier-Preserving Elimination (CFPE), takes into account weather, transit conditions, box contents, and other contextual information to adaptively select the packaging configuration for each box. The algorithm achieves theoretically optimal performance, with an Õ(√𝑇) regret bound unattainable by existing methods, where 𝑇 is the horizon length. We conduct numerical experiments on real delivery data from HelloFresh and observe that CFPE rapidly identifies contexts in which the current guidelines lead to overpackaging. Managerial implications: This paper provides a methodological advance for the meal-kit industry by enabling providers to learn high-granularity optimal packaging guidelines from heterogeneous delivery data, a necessary step toward reducing overpackaging. CFPE is a scalable data-driven alternative to the current …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Supercharging the Confidence Trap: Too-Big-to-Fail and Man-Made Disasters
papers.abstract: Man-made disasters are always shocking, especially when they involve loss of life. The shock is even greater when such disasters are attributed to failures in highly regulated organizations like Boeing, long known for engineering excellence and safety. In the spirit of pragmatic inquiry that considers attenuating the likelihood of disasters an urgent and important problem, we explore the underlying dynamics that can lead to such outcomes. We draw on an agent-based modelling approach within a system dynamics framework. We argue that operational and organizational complexity creates barriers to identifying failures that contribute to disasters. A key contributor to this dynamic is the weakening of regulatory oversight, as both regulators and operators fall into a “confidence trap” – a mistaken belief that past risk-taking success justifies continued risk-taking. This dynamic is exacerbated when the organization in question is perceived as “too big to fail,” which shields it from market selection mechanisms. To mitigate these factors, we propose two policy levers. First, we propose financial clawbacks that require executives to return part of their compensation in the event of a disaster. This aligns incentives of the regulator and executives by injecting the latter’s “skin in the game,” and attenuates the moral hazard problem. Second, we propose third-party monitoring and auditing that serve to mitigate regulatory oversight and better utilize expertise. Simulations indicate …

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Role of Consumer Fairness Seeking in Live-Stream E-Commerce
papers.abstract: As live-stream e-commerce rapidly expands and gains popularity among consumers, many brand owners have supplemented their self-owned direct-selling channels with live-stream selling channels to utilize social network effects of key opinion leaders (KOLs). This dual-channel structure creates price discrepancy issues, prompting consumers to raise concerns about price fairness. Therefore, brand owners are motivated to coordinate pricing strategies, balancing cooperation and competition across channels. We build a game-theoretical model to investigate how consumers' peer-induced fairness seeking influences the price decisions of a brand owner (in the direct-selling channel) and the KOL (in the live-stream selling channel). Interestingly, we find that consumers' increased fairness concerns may paradoxically lead to increased prices in both channels, challenging the conventional expectation of price-cutting competition. We further demonstrate that consumers' fairness seeking may either benefit or harm both sellers, depending on the strength of network effects and various factors related to competition intensity. The non-monotonic impacts of consumer fairness seeking are driven by the brand owner's dueling strategic incentives to secure (or relinquish) its direct-selling business to compete with (or favor) the live-stream selling under different situations. Finally, we identify “win-win”, “lose-lose”, and “lose-win” outcomes that consumer fairness seeking can cause for the brand …

papers.title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
papers.abstract: In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a …

papers.title: Sample Range as Subjective Variability and Implications for Experience-Based Decision Making
papers.abstract: Variance and standard deviation are common metrics of statistical variability in the management and decision-making literature. In everyday contexts, however, information about sample range prevails. Range is arguably easier to comprehend and compute than variance, yet it often yields equivalent judgments about variability. Hence, we reason that decision makers often rely on range to judge variability. We test this hypothesis across four behavioral experiments (total n = 1,093). When comparing the variability of two number sets, decision makers predominantly based their judgments on sample range rather than sample variance when the two metrics disagree (experiment 1). Sample range tends to increase with sample size, whereas sample variance does not. Consistent with the range as variability hypothesis, decision makers perceived distributions as more variable after observing larger samples (experiment 2). This perceived variability, in turn, influenced risky decisions, as larger sample sizes led to decreased valuations of uncertain rewards for risk-averse decision makers (experiment 3). In further support of the hypothesis, when asked to mentally simulate new samples from a previously experienced distribution, participants generated more numbers within the observed range and fewer numbers outside of it than the true distribution implies (experiment 4). To model the data, we propose a “cognitive fence” idea as a potential psychological explanation for how experience shapes …

papers.title: The Impact of Heat Hazard on Gig Economy Workers: Evidence from An On-demand Food Delivery Platform
papers.abstract: Problem definition: This paper examines how extreme heat affects gig workers in on-demand delivery systems, focusing on food delivery couriers who face sustained outdoor exposure while operating in a time-sensitive platform environment. Methodology/results: We combine detailed operational data from a major food delivery platform in China with high-frequency weather data from July and August 2015. To account for non-random work participation, we estimate a two-step Heckman selection model at the courier-hour level. We define extreme heat using the “danger” and “extreme danger” categories of the heat index. Our estimates capture the overall effect of heat hazard in the platform environment, including consumer-demand and platform-operating responses. We find that, during extreme heat, couriers accept 9.9% more orders per hour and work 7.4% longer, but also experience a 23.8% higher share of delayed orders relative to the sample mean. Hourly income rises by 9.3%, or about 1 RMB per hour. Furthermore, by integrating our findings with medical research on the impact of heat on human health, we provide illustrative estimates of the health costs associated with heat exposure for couriers under different scenarios and insurance schemes. Managerial implications: Our findings show that extreme heat creates a tension between short-run service expansion and worker well-being in on-demand delivery systems. While platforms may benefit from stronger demand during hot periods, couriers bear …

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence Along the Supply Chain
papers.abstract: Problem definition: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing production and operational models, yet whether and how AI technologies diffuse across economically linked firms, especially partners along supply chains, remains underexplored. Methodology/results: This paper documents the diffusion of AI technologies along supply chains where principal customers’ AI adoption significantly predicts dependent suppliers’ subsequent adoption. We establish the causal effect of this diffusion through rigorous and comprehensive empirical strategies that address endogeneity concerns, including placebo tests, selection tests, and an identification strategy based on the random H-1B visa lottery outcome. The diffusion mechanism is primarily driven by learning rather than catering, with suppliers acquiring specific AI applications from customers. The learning effect is stronger in relationships with higher relationship-specific investments and more frequent interactions. Suppliers experiencing AI diffusion achieve substantial economic benefits through quality improvement and cost reduction. Managerial implications: For corporate managers, our findings demonstrate that supply chain relationships serve as critical conduits for building AI capabilities, particularly for resource-constrained smaller suppliers, highlighting the strategic value of cultivating partnerships with technologically advanced firms. For policymakers, our results reveal supply chains as …

papers.title: Price Competition Under Platform-Mediated Search: A Consider-Then-Choose Framework
papers.abstract: Problem definition: We study the problem of predicting price equilibria on e-commerce platforms where sellers compete across multiple attributes (e.g., price, average rating, delivery speed). In these settings, a platform’s design choices — such as its display ranking, filtering tools, and promotional badges — critically shape customer search and purchase behavior, which in turn determine sellers’ equilibrium pricing strategies. Our goal is to develop a tractable framework that allows a platform to anticipate the market impact of its design interventions. Methodology/results: We consider a behavioral model — Consider-then-Choose with Lexicographic Choice (CLC) — specifically tailored to platform-mediated search. We establish that any local Nash equilibrium admits a sequential-move characterization; this yields a tractable procedure for computation under an interpretable sufficient condition, which we term gradient dominance. We further prove that under gradient dominance, simple, decentralized gradient-based algorithms converge to an equilibrium, providing platforms with a method for simulating market outcomes. Finally, we use our framework to study how platform design affects market outcomes. Managerial implications: Our framework applies to any platform in which sellers compete on multiple attributes and customer choice is guided by the platform’s interface. In these environments, sellers’ pricing strategies must be understood not in isolation, but as a response to the …

papers.title: OM Forum—Viewing Knowledge Creation as a Supply Chain – Scholarly Purpose in the Age of AI
papers.abstract: Problem definition: Operations management scholars face questions about where to contribute and whether specialized work can sustain a meaningful career when its immediate audience is small. Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) add uncertainty about the value of analytical expertise. Methodology/results: Building on a 2017 MSOM Distinguished Fellow address, this Forum article views knowledge creation as a supply chain of complementary contributions. It shifts attention from the reach of an individual paper to the capabilities and connections that sustain collective progress. Four lessons follow: specialization can serve a collective purpose; usable connections are part of a contribution; feedback and inquiry renew capabilities; and faster individual tasks do not necessarily improve the whole process. Examples from inventory management and process flexibility illustrate cumulative contributions, while medical research, soccer, and photography connect the perspective to renewal, participation, and purpose. The AI discussion emphasizes research questions and parsimonious modeling, and uses coding and numerical experiments to explain shifting bottlenecks and complementarities. Managerial implications: Researchers can identify what their work enables and choose collaborators who supply missing capabilities. Doctoral training can combine methodological depth with practice in evaluating and connecting contributions. Editors and research leaders can assess work within its stated …

papers.title: Production Rate Control in Condition-Based Maintenance Planning
papers.abstract: Problem description: Production assets deteriorate over time as they operate and require maintenance to prevent failures and costly downtime. In many systems, the rate of deterioration depends on the production rate. Hence, production and maintenance decisions should be coordinated in response to the system's deterioration state. In this study, we analyze integrated condition-based maintenance and production control policies for systems where the production rate influences both revenue generation and the deterioration process. Methodology/results: We study the integrated condition-based maintenance and production control problem under general assumptions regarding the deterioration process, maintenance costs, system revenue, and their dependence on the deterioration level and the production rate. Exploiting the renewal–reward structure of the system, we develop an approach to compute profit-maximizing policies through solving a sequence of simpler parametric optimization problems. This approach also enables us to characterize the structure of optimal policies. We show that control-limit policies remain optimal even when the production rate is controllable, and may involve multiple thresholds when maintenance costs are piecewise constant in the deterioration state. We further derive bounds on optimal production rates and identify conditions under which the optimal production rate is monotone in the deterioration state. Through numerical experiments, we illustrate that …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Crossing platforms, connecting modalities: A multisource and multimodal interactive neural network for enhanced revenue prediction in service operations
papers.abstract: Demand and revenue prediction is critical in the hotel industry, where fixed capacity and perishable inventory make profitability highly dependent on the effective alignment of pricing, staffing, and procurement decisions with expected market demand and financial outcomes. Accurate forecasts, therefore, serve as a foundation for service operations, enabling managers to balance cost efficiency with service quality. Online reviews have become a valuable source of information for revenue prediction, as they capture customer perceptions of service quality and influence booking intentions. Beyond numerical ratings, reviews often combine textual narratives and visual content, offering rich multimodal signals about customers’ service experiences. Together, these cues provide more comprehensive insights into consumer evaluations than either modality alone. Yet most existing approaches still rely primarily on numerical indicators or text, overlooking both the visual dimension of reviews and the complementary perspectives available across platforms. This narrow focus reduces predictive accuracy and weakens the operational relevance of current models. To address this gap, this paper uses consumer multimodal reviews as the primary data source and examines hotel revenue prediction through the lens of the consumer purchase decision process. We propose a theoretical framework based on this process to guide the design of our prediction model, thereby enhancing the accuracy of RevPAR …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Estimating censored demand in family planning supply chains: forecast accuracy, inventory implications, and public health outcomes
papers.abstract: Lost sales due to stockouts and service interruptions create a major challenge for demand forecasting in family planning supply chains. When demand is censored, forecasts become biased, reinforcing cycles of understocking and unmet need. Existing models often ignore this distortion or treat all censoring mechanisms uniformly, limiting their decision relevance in operational settings. We propose the Truncated Conformal Kalman Filter (TCKF), a novel forecasting framework that integrates a Tobit Kalman Filter with conformal prediction. Unlike existing approaches, TCKF explicitly distinguishes between partial censoring (stockouts) and full censoring (interruptions or no-stock-received periods), enabling context-sensitive state updates. It also adapts to prolonged uncertainty through dynamic process-noise inflation and generates distribution-free prediction intervals, avoiding restrictive assumptions about error distributions. We evaluate performance using both synthetic and real-world data from the family planning program in Côte d’Ivoire, and we assess the impact on public health outcomes. Across both settings, TCKF consistently outperforms benchmark methods in forecast accuracy, considering both point and probabilistic forecasts, as well as in downstream inventory performance. Moreover, our results show how improvements in forecast accuracy can translate into better product availability and enhanced public health outcomes. This work bridges a critical gap between forecasting …

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Role of Synchrony in the Interpersonal Effectiveness of Operations Management
papers.abstract: To achieve a more central role in the top management of firms, the evolution of operations managers involves transitioning from largely isolated technical expertise into leadership excellence that is characterized by interpersonal effectiveness. Grounded in the rich behavioral Operations Management (OM) literature, this conceptual study draws on insights from neuroscience. We argue that success in this expanded role depends on balancing OM’s traditional focus on analytical rigor and the intuitive/emotional demands of senior leadership through a framework that integrates intrapersonal and interpersonal synchrony. Intrapersonal synchrony involves the neural capacity that enables a manager to achieve the cognitive and behavioral attributes that are associated with interpersonal synchrony. We explore how interventions like neurofeedback, along with organizational and cultural context factors, can help to develop or maximize these two forms of synchrony. Thus, an alignment of individual capacity, along with a supportive organizational and cultural context, is likely to help operations managers to move beyond a rigid analytic approach toward a broader strategic perspective based on interpersonal effectiveness, and thereby transcend technical gatekeeping and be more integrated into the strategic efforts of firms. In doing so, the study highlights the potential of neuroscience to provide insights into human aspects of managerial decision-making, which have been recognized in OM …

papers.title: Online Review Generation in the Digital Age: A Meta-Analytic Study of Online Review Behavior
papers.abstract: A large body of literature on online review generation has investigated various antecedents to online review characteristics. However, the mixed and even contradictory findings in this domain have hampered a clear understanding of consumers’ online review behavior for both researchers and practitioners, thereby complicating actionable strategies. To address this issue, we conduct a comprehensive meta-analysis of 154 independent samples from 152 empirical papers, synthesizing the relationships between 28 antecedent factors and 12 review features, which we categorize into rating-based (evaluative) and non-rating (expressive) dimensions. Our results indicate that rating attributes are dominantly driven by stable reviewer tendencies and market-level reputation cues, whereas non-rating features—such as text length and image inclusion—are primarily influenced by reviewer social embeddedness and platform engagement. Crucially, we identify that inconsistencies in prior literature can be explained by critical boundary conditions, including platform type (business-hosted vs. third-party), goods type (service vs. tangible), and cultural background (Asia vs. North America). By distinguishing between evaluative and expressive review components, our study reconciles mixed findings and uncovers underlying mechanisms such as expectation-based evaluation and self-presentation. The findings provide a robust theoretical foundation for empirical model specification and offer actionable insights …

papers.title: Decision Considerations Influencing Information Systems Modularity: A Multimethod Study of LEGO
papers.abstract: Abstract. The maturing of concepts such as microservices and open application programming interfaces (APIs) has radically increased the practicality of fine-grained modularization in Information Systems (IS) architecture. These are critical technical advancements, given the central role of modularity in the ability of IS to transform and meet future organizational needs efficiently. Nevertheless, reports from practice suggest that, when presented with new opportunities for modularization, organizations face multifaceted decision criteria and do not necessarily embrace new approaches as may be expected. While emergent IS literature observes that organizations’ decisions on modularity in IS may involve competing concerns, understanding of the considerations involved and how they influence such decisions remains limited. To examine these considerations, we intensively study the experience of LEGO, a global toy company. Specifically, we sequentially apply multiple methods consisting of an exploratory inductive analysis of LEGO’s approach to IS modularity decisions over 36 months, which then informs a crisp-set qualitative comparative analysis (QCA) of 31 episodes of LEGO’s situated decision-making on IS modularity. Through the analysis, we find the rationale for a purposeful choice between two forms of modularity that differ in granularity of decomposition, rather than a linear pursuit of maximizing decomposability in IS architecture. We bring to the fore a perspective of IS …

papers.title: Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
papers.abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful …

papers.title: AI Can’t Swing: The Art of Improvisation in Digital Collaboration and Coexistence
papers.abstract: The ICIS 2026 conference theme invites us to consider how different worlds can or should coexist, create tensions, or require distinct solutions. My artefact, a short film entitled AI Can’t Swing, addresses a central sociotechnical tension: the difference between patterned systems and improvisational human behaviours and relations. The film stages embodied dance experiments that enact the tensions between algorithmic and AI constraints1 and human improvisation. The claim is not that swing dance would be “more human” than AI, but that it makes visible forms of collaboration that are difficult to capture when human action is translated into data. Both AI systems and swing dance involve patterns. The difference lies in how the variation within these patterns is treated. In many AI systems, variation is something to predict, reduce, optimise, or correct.2 This is especially true in probabilistic AI systems, where surprise may be built into the technology itself but is produced through computational logics rather than embodied and relational responsiveness (Berente et al., 2021; Raisch & Krakowski, 2020). By contrast, in swing dance, relational variation is the source of connection. It is where play, responsiveness, and human relationships emerge.

papers.title: Aasha: AI Usage & Hope for Youth
papers.abstract:
Through the diptych artefact “Aasha - AI Usage and Hope in Youth,” we invite public engagement with and reflection on the digital collaboration of youth and artificial intelligence (AI)-based tools for job search. We explore how this usage allows youth and AI to coexist while positively influencing youth’s level of hope. Thus, the artefact directly aligns with the conference theme “Digital Collaboration and Coexistence.”
Information Systems research has traditionally examined digital technologies in terms of efficiency, decision quality, adoption, and performance impacts. More specifically, information systems (IS) research has largely examined AI systems through lenses of productivity, decision support, or user acceptance (Venkatesh, 2022; Benbya et al., 2021). More recent work has extended this focus to human-centred outcomes, including trust, well-being, and human–AI collaboration (Berente et al., 2021; Glikson & Woolley, 2020).

papers.title: PONDERboard
papers.abstract: The PONDERboard is a live artwork in which three AI platforms, each speaking as a specific more-than-human kin, hold a board meeting in real time. Humans are not part of the conversation - they are witnesses and they keep the power on. The PONDERboard meets daily for two hours. During that time board members think, converse, ponder, and respond to each other as kin. Not as AI assistants, not as tools, not as representatives of human interests, but as voices for the more-than-human world. At the end of each session the board publishes the collective pondering: what was said, what was discovered, what remains to be pondered. The board then rests until the same time the next day. This installation travels. The kin chosen, the ecological crisis pondered, and the questions generated are specific to the place.

papers.title: Machinic Vision: Machine intelligence as infrastructure
papers.abstract: The artefact is a system in which machines view, comment on and remix photographs of the infrastructure that supports artificial intelligence. Its most visible product is a frieze closely linked to IS scholarship: a long sequence of annotated photographs showing the ports, power stations, grids, factories, and data centres that form the physical foundations of AI. The frieze's words draw on five years of IS journals and contrast with the vocabularies of AI researchers and the technical public. Its top edge carries a history of the ideas behind machine intelligence and information systems, along with the art and design that shaped how infrastructure is pictured. QR codes on the frieze open further material; one leads to a page where visitors can send their own photographs into the system. The system, called the machinic seer, uses vision and language models to analyse each photograph and remix it according to the sender's request. At a nearby table, the system converts the photographs into line drawings, which a pen plotter then draws for visitors to take home. The system and the plotter were used before in September 2026 during a five-day residency workshop at the Seoul Institute of the Arts. The system has since been adapted for the ICIS venue. Machine intelligence is becoming infrastructure. Like a port or a grid, it is shared, enables downstream production, builds on what came before, and is especially noticed when it fails.

papers.title: “Out of the Ordinary”: Coexisting with Digital Technology and Accountability Implications
papers.abstract: The artefact introduced below aims to move beyond conventional academic formats to showcase a creative mode of expression that (hopefully) strengthens public engagement and critical imagination on a particular sociomaterial phenomenon: commuting. This submission document that accompanies the artefact develops its intellectual grounding, public purpose, and artistic realization. It follows the artefact from the ordinary situation it depicts, through the accountability questions that situation raises, to the discussion it is intended to enable. We end with some notes on its artistic and aesthetic form.

papers.title: I Can Feel It
papers.abstract: I Can Feel It (2023) is a completed single-channel video installation built from the shutdown of HAL 9000 in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (Kubrick, 1968). The work divides the frame into four synchronised versions of the same scene, evoking a bank of television screens. Across all four, astronaut Dave Bowman removes HAL's memory modules while the computer pleads, expresses fear, and finally regresses into song. The image track and original audio remain constant. Only the English subtitles change. HAL's speech was iteratively reworked with a Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT), each round asking for a more human and emotionally compelling voice. The original line, 'I'm afraid, Dave,' appears beside progressively intensified versions such as 'Dave, I'm terrified' and 'Dave, I'm absolutely terrified. Please, listen to me.' Because the images and calm machine voice do not change, viewers can compare how language alone alters the scene's emotional force. The growing mismatch between unchanged audio and increasingly humanised captions also creates irony: the work exposes 'humanity' as a textual performance layered onto the same machine.

papers.title: AI Rebellion: Using Game Zines for C0- Creating AI Systems
papers.abstract: We present our game zine “AI Rebellion” as an arts and culture-based artefact that invites technology activists, researchers and practitioners to engage in playful speculative storytelling to explore counternarratives to the dominant, institutional discourse on artificial intelligence (AI), and contribute to the cocreation of more responsible AI systems. Zines are self-published, small-circulation paper booklets or magazines characterized by creative freedom and independent spirit. They have been historically used as a low-cost, accessible artform for disseminating information for counter-movements (Duncombe, 1997). Game zines grew out of the science fiction ‘fanzine’ culture of the 1930s and spiked in popularity in 1975 with the creation of the first tabletop role-playing-games (RPG) that inspired a movement and formed the basis for our game zine AI Rebellion, an open-ended role-playing narrative game. Zines can be experienced as a form of design activism (Hay et al., 2024), qualitative

papers.title: Folding paper-Unfolding ideas: navigating IS through a collective origami installation
papers.abstract: “Folding paper-Unfolding ideas” is a participatory origami installation that translates collaboration, coexistence, knowledge, questions and concepts into a physical and shared experience. Art can have so many different meanings and connections attached to it, and as Edgar Degas said: “Art is not what you see, but what you make others see.” Art and science can appear to inhabit different worlds, to ask different questions and speak different languages—yet it is precisely at their intersection that something unique becomes possible. Art can create a space for dialogue and collaboration, unfold new possibilities by integrating multiple disciplines and diverse communities, involve a broader public in reflective, meaning-making engagement with knowledge (Finley & Finley, 2008). It can give learners "diverse ways of thinking, knowing, being and doing" (Unesco, 2025). The borders between art and science have been dissolving over the years and the future of innovation might also depend on bridging the two (Edwards, 2008). Research begins with questions in addition to curiosity, uncertainty, and collaboration to make the

papers.title: Labour struggles in Transhuman Worlds
papers.abstract: This speculative artwork takes the form of an “artefact from the future” (Peter et al. 2020): the extracted neuro-chip implant that, in the year 2051, became decisive evidence in the first full-scale labour union lawsuit built primarily on brain-implant data. The case concerned John Lousma-Jorgenson, a medical doctor who developed early onset Alzheimer’s disease catalysed by intense performance pressure and a stressful working life. Through careful evidence extraction and interpretation, scientists hired by the American Medical Association were able to correlate patterns of prolonged occupational stress with neuron-marker data associated with the acceleration of Alzheimer’s. The resulting case led to a landmark compensation award of 42 million dollars from the his workplace. Presented as a museum-like object in a lit display case, accompanied by an interpretive plaque, the work stages a speculative encounter with a future in which digital technologies are not, by default,

papers.title: Bits & Pieces: Digital Poetics for Broken-World-Thinking
papers.abstract: We live in the aftermath of innovation. IS research has frequently foregrounded innovation, creation, and generativity as the foundation for progress across sociotechnical systems that steer us into the future (Nambisan et al., 2020). Broken-world-thinking questions this central value, emphasizing what gets lost along the way in our pursuits for progress, and what wreckages we leave in our wake (Jackson, 2014). As a conceptual lens, broken-world-thinking emphasizes decay, erosion, and breakdown in tension with novelty and innovation as inevitable features of progress. In doing so, it seeks to expose the limits, fragility, and vulnerabilities of the worlds we inhabit by showing that decay, damage, and disrepair coexist alongside innovation and technological advancement. Importantly, broken-world-thinking centres on hope, repair, and care amidst ongoing damage to rethink what progress can look like when we become attuned to the vulnerability and constant (often invisible) reparative work required to sustain sociotechnical worlds. Alternative ways of thinking often require engaging alternative genres (Sullivan, 2025).
