Specifically, this project engages in poetics as “interpretatively flexible poetry” to study sociotechnical phenomena (Sarker et al., 2018, p. 763).

papers.title: The AI We Choose: Deploy Before It Breaks! A Playable Experiment in Work, Power, and Digital Coexistence
papers.abstract: The AI We Choose is an interactive physical board game about introducing artificial intelligence (AI) into working life without breaking the social conditions that make collaboration possible. It responds to the ICIS 2026 theme by turning coexistence into a playable challenge. Participants form an AI project team led by Maya, the Project Lead, and challenged by Victor, the company’s CEO, to deploy a new system in ten fictional weeks. Success requires more than technical delivery: the team must protect worker trust, create accountability, and keep the project alive under executive pressure. The central question is: Can we build AI-enabled work without exhausting people, reproducing injustice, or making consequential decisions impossible to contest?

papers.title: Artful Routes: On Human-Algorithm Collaboration
papers.abstract: Artful Routes is an interactive generative-art project that explores what happens when an information-processing algorithm designed for optimization is repositioned as a creative and cultural medium. The project uses an algorithm designed for the Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) to create complex shapes humans can transform into digital artefacts. Finding the shortest route between multiple locations is a well-known challenge in mathematics, computer science and information systems (Cook, 2012). The number of possible routes grows factorially for each additional stop, making it impossible to test every option in a reasonable amount of computing time. Consequently, Artful Routes uses a probabilistic algorithm to find short routes efficiently. While these routes are not necessarily the shortest possible, they provide efficient TSP routes without requiring excessive time. The software developed for the project can be accessed by participants through a web browser. The system generates 100 randomly positioned points which participants can watch being processed in real time. The resulting unique shapes can be named and submitted to the project's shared database. This is where the human element of the artistic process begins: participants use the TSP-generated shapes as raw material for creative expression, transforming them through creative coding techniques such as fill, curve, rotate, scale, layer, and colour. The proposition of Artful Routes is not that the TSP itself is …

papers.title: The Last Draft
papers.abstract: Generative AI is frequently framed through the productivity lens (Gopal et al., 2025; Wessel et al., 2025). This project translates this into an intimate creative setting. It explores the tension of potential displacement of human creative agency (Benbya et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2025). If creative systems can increasingly perform the cognitive activities associated with creativity, humans may confront questions of authorship, identity, and dignity (Jensen et al., 2025). This idea draws artistic inspiration from Charlie Chaplin's Modern Times. Chaplin transformed anxieties surrounding industrial automation into visual comedy in which a worker gradually becomes subordinated to the machinery designed to improve production (Kamin, 2008). The historical parallel is deliberate. The industrial machine mechanized physical labor, while generative AI increasingly reaches into cognitive and creative labor. In both cases, technological progress raises the question of whether humans control their tools or gradually reorganize themselves around them.

papers.title: Aesthetic Enactments in the Age of Performing Machines
papers.abstract: This artefact, staged as a live performance, brings together piano, wine, and their digital counterparts in a shared sensory encounter. Guided by a concert pianist and a professional sommelier, the audience is invited to listen, taste, guess, and reflect on what changes when, in the age of AI, the presence of a human becomes uncertain. What does it mean to sense a human presence in an experience? Why does that presence seem to matter, and what, exactly, are we sensing when we believe it is there?

papers.title: FromTativille to AIville
papers.abstract: Playtime is Jacques Tati's fourth and most ambitious film, a nearly dialogue-free comedy that follows his recurring character Monsieur Hulot. As he wanders through a hyper-modern Paris, Hulot is constantly baffled by the "smart" technology of his time: doors that don't open when they should, furniture that is uncomfortable, and elevators that separate rather than connect people. Characters get lost in glass corridors, mistake reflections for reality, and struggle with furniture and machines that seem to counter comfort or intuition. Playtime is a comedy, but it is also a brilliant critique: how architecture and technology shape (and sometimes sabotage) the people who live with them. Today, as we navigate the world of Generative AI, we find ourselves living in our own version of "Tativille" - one structured not by glass walls and office blocks alone, but by interfaces, prompts, algorithms, and hallucinations. The mechanisms of influence remain pervasive, yet they have become even more invisible.

papers.title: Puddle: Learning to Move as Water
papers.abstract: Puddle is an interactive installation built around a large screen and camera-based body tracking. One participant at a time stands in a circle marked on the floor in front of the screen and controls a water-body with their own posture: bending forward, leaning to the side, crouching and moving the arms. This waterbody becomes their only visible body in the virtual environment, responding continuously to their physical movement.

papers.title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
papers.abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .

papers.title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
papers.abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% …

papers.title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
papers.abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the …

papers.title: Connectors and Influencers
papers.abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by H2020 Future and Emerging Technologies [IBSEN Contract 662725]; the Keynes Fund, University of Cambridge; and the Creative-Pioneering Researchers Program, Seoul National University. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07308 .

papers.title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
papers.abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In …

papers.title: You cannot not communicate: opt-out features and targeting with ML-based recommender systems
papers.abstract: With the rise of machine learning (ML), consumers’ personal data is widely used for personalized product recommendations. To address privacy concerns, regulations increasingly grant consumers control over their data. One popular implementation is the “opt-out of information use” feature which allows consumers to specify which of their collected personal data recommender systems can harness. However, we conjecture that such features may have an unintended side effect: withholding data could inadvertently reveal insights about consumers’ latent characteristics, thereby enhancing targeting possibilities. Through a controlled experiment, we evaluate both consumers’ perceptions and technical consequences of such opt-out features in the context of a typical search problem for which we train an ML-based recommender. Our results show that these features increase consumers’ sense of control over the system and reduce perceived privacy intrusion among those who actually withhold information. Paradoxically, withholding information can simultaneously be harnessed to improve the ML model’s predictive accuracy. From a regulatory perspective, we highlight the need for specifying rules on how organizations may use information withholding decisions when consumers’ interests conflict with those of the recommender provider.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Digital Platforms Meet Artificial Intelligence: Implications for POM Research and Practice
papers.abstract: Digital platforms are changing how firms design, coordinate, and govern operations by integrating artificial intelligence, blockchain, digital sensing and digital twins, data infrastructure, and additive manufacturing. This paper develops a forward-looking research agenda for production and operations management by distinguishing enabling technologies from the platforms, workflows, and business models through which they are deployed. We organize the agenda around a sequence linking technological capability, operational manifestation, mechanism, outcomes, and boundary conditions. The relevant mechanisms include prediction, information visibility, verification, orchestration, monitoring, human override, and decision rights. We articulate how these mechanisms may create operational value through improvements in productivity, quality, responsiveness, resilience, compliance, and customer experience, enabling firms to capture financial value through revenue growth, cost reduction, risk avoidance, and improved asset utilization. We identify enduring operations management themes that emerging technologies may reshape, and develop five forward-looking paths involving artificial intelligence-enabled business-to-business platforms, physical–digital integration, agentic service workflows, data and artificial intelligence governance, and platform-enabled resilience under geopolitical disruption. Finally, we discuss theoretical and methodological approaches that can support cumulative …

papers.title: EXPRESS: Bounded Rationality in Public Healthcare Competition
papers.abstract: Fiscal pressure forces public healthcare systems to reduce waiting times via hospital competition, yet patients' bounded rationality weakens this policy. We develop a Hotelling-type queueing model that incorporates the strategic interaction between two budget-constrained public hospitals and patients with heterogeneous preferences and bounded rationality. Our analysis yields the following results. First, we show that bounded rationality can incentivize hospitals to increase service rates, thereby alleviating congestion and leading to an inverted-U relationship between patient welfare and the degree of bounded rationality. Moreover, the effect of bounded rationality on hospital revenue is also non-monotonic: when the capacity constraint is tight and the budget is sufficiently high, hospital revenue may be maximized at an intermediate level of bounded rationality rather than under full rationality. Second, higher reimbursement does not necessarily enhance patient welfare; instead, we identify an optimal reimbursement level that rises with the available public budget. Third, extending the framework to a multi-hospital environment within a Salop model shows that total market share, patient welfare, and hospital revenue are all maximized at a moderate level of competition. Overall, from a managerial perspective, healthcare managers should carefully account for patients' bounded rationality when designing capacity and information disclosure policies. Meanwhile, excessive hospital …

papers.title: EXPRESS: An Exploratory Analysis of Variation in Payback Periods of Emissions Reduction Projects Using CDP Disclosures
papers.abstract: Firms continue to engage in projects to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions. Based on their disclosures to CDP, many such projects have relatively short payback periods of 2-3 years. Earlier work by Blanco et al. (2020) found that payback periods appeared stable over time between 2010-2016. The current paper extends that work in several directions: by using a substantially longer time horizon, and exploring several factors that contribute to the variation in payback periods and trends. With the longer horizon of data now available, we find that paybacks are lengthening slowly but significantly over 2010-2024, by an average of about 2 weeks per year, or approximately one half year over our 14-year horizon. Firms with greater liabilities relative to their assets report faster payback, though the effect is only marginally significant. Firms in Europe that are subject to a carbon tax or an emissions trading scheme report shorter paybacks than in the US or elsewhere. Firms that are more consumer-facing report lengthening payback periods, while upstream firms do not. This analysis is exploratory, but prior firm-level research on these effects is mixed and surprisingly limited.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Dynamic Principal-Agent Problem in Queueing Systems with Customer Abandonment
papers.abstract: Service systems in which demand, congestion, and worker incentives evolve jointly are ubiquitous in modern operations. We study a dynamic principal–agent problem in a queueing system with customer abandonment, where the principal controls arrivals through pricing and the agent privately chooses a costly service rate. Modeling workload as a controlled reflected diffusion, we characterize the centralized and decentralized Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equations and construct a representative two-part contract consisting of an access charge and a completion payment. Under unrestricted transfers, the contract coordinates pricing and service to attain the first-best joint payoff. Whenever participation is feasible, it makes the agent's participation constraint bind and allocates the remaining surplus to the principal. Implementation is robust to misspecification of the service-rate function used by the principal. We also establish conditions under which the representative payment schedules are nonmonotone in workload. Extensions consider multiple agents, general patience distributions, and information disclosure in a reduced Bayesian-persuasion benchmark. Numerical examples illustrate how the effects of customer impatience on optimal pricing and service can vary with congestion.

papers.title: The Workplace GenAI Usage Divide: A Genetics-Informed Cognitive and Metacognitive Account
papers.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is increasingly deployed in organizations, yet employees differ substantially and persistently in how frequently and intensively they use it. This workplace “usage divide” raises a fundamental but underexplored question: Why do employees differ systematically in their use of GenAI, even under common formal access? We argue that this divide reflects a broader challenge for IS research: explaining the use of systems that are probabilistic rather than deterministic, and general-purpose yet uneven and evolving in their capabilities. In workplaces where employees remain accountable for task performance, these properties make the use of GenAI not a routine adoption decision but a judgment process in which employees assess the system’s credibility and determine where task-relevant expertise lies. Drawing on molecular genetics and metacognition research, we theorize that genetic propensity, indexed by the educational attainment polygenic score (PGS)—an aggregate genetic index associated with educational attainment—helps account for systematic variation in these judgments and, ultimately, persistent differences in workplace GenAI use. Specifically, we develop a parsimonious two-pathway model linking educational attainment PGS to GenAI use: a cognitive pathway involving formal educational attainment and perceptions of GenAI credibility, and a metacognitive pathway involving strategic mindset and metaknowledge of where task-relevant expertise lies. We test our …

papers.title: The Interplay of Digital and Physical Materialities in IT Affordances: A Study of Governance of Controlled Medications in a Hospital
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT In studies of information technology (IT) in organizations, affordance theory may be used to explain what possibilities for action IT offers, under what conditions they are actualized and how they shape action and outcomes. Affordance theory suggests that materiality matters because it furnishes possibilities for action. However, in studies of IT affordances, the digital and physical materialities of IT are usually in focus, while the physical materiality of non‐IT artefacts is seldom considered. This paper examines how the physical materiality of non‐IT artefacts conditions the action possibilities an IT system offers its users. We base our observations on a study of IT implemented in a hospital to improve visibility and accountability of the use of controlled drugs, such as opioids. We compare how the materiality of both IT and paper‐based systems used for these purposes interplays with the materiality of the medications and other non‐IT artefacts in nurses and pharmacists' accountability work. We found different combinations of technologies and medications, condition visibility for the organization in different ways, with distinct ways of knowing about medication work, and different potential accountability outcomes. Temporal processes of accountability work, such as recurrence, accumulation or temporal lag, also condition different outcomes of affordance actualization. Overall, by illuminating material and temporal influences behind visibility and potential for …

papers.title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
papers.abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we …

papers.title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
papers.abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge support from the FRIC Center for Financial Frictions [Grant DNRF102]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09038 .

papers.title: EXPRESS: Benefits of Extreme Political Stability and Instability of Supplier Countries for Firms: The U-Shaped Relationship
papers.abstract: Using a large-scale panel dataset of U.S. buyer firms and their global supplier networks from 2010 to 2020, we examine how global political instability (GPI), a firm’s weighted exposure to political instability across the countries where its international suppliers operate, is associated with firm performance. We find a U-shaped relationship: buyer firm performance is highest when a firm's overall sourcing exposure reflects either very low or very high levels of GPI. At the low-GPI end, the results align with transaction-cost economics (TCE), as political stability is associated with lower uncertainty and fewer coordination frictions. At the very high-GPI end, we identify bargaining power as a key mechanism: buyers exposed to politically unstable supplier countries exhibit greater bargaining power and more favorable contractual terms, particularly favorable trade credit, which may partially offset the costs of political instability. We further show that this nonlinear relationship varies across industries. It is more pronounced in productive industries, where buyers have greater bargaining power to negotiate favorable trade credit and lower switching costs to reallocate sourcing during periods of political instability. However, it is flatter in durable-goods industries, where asset specificity and higher switching costs are associated with weaker bargaining power and a more limited ability to secure favorable trade credit from suppliers in politically unstable countries. …

papers.title: Incumbents’ Alliances and (Non-)Adaptation During the Pre-Commercialization Stage of a New Technology
papers.abstract: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets. This assumption fits the commercialization stage of a new technology, when both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets hold high value. However, during the pre-commercialization stage—when proprietary knowledge in the new technology is valuable but incumbents’ complementary assets cannot yet be fully deployed to commercialize the new technology—this logic may not hold. We develop a framework that explains how stage-dependent shifts in the value of both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets alter the bargaining power between incumbents and knowledge-possessing firms, thereby reshaping the adaptive potential of alliances. Using data on the semiconductor industry during the emergence of nanotechnology, we found that alliances between semiconductor incumbents and nanotechnology-capable partners are less likely to form and, even when formed, are less likely to focus on the explicit transfer of proprietary knowledge in emerging nanotechnology. Moreover, these alliances are more likely to be structured as joint ventures, especially when the risk of knowledge leakage is heightened. Joint venture arrangements, in turn, impede semiconductor incumbents’ post-alliance nanotechnology invention more than contractual arrangements. Taken together, we develop insights …

papers.title: Wrongdoers or Saviors? CEO Activism, Media Partisanship, and the Media’s Construction of CEO Infamy and Celebrity
papers.abstract: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles. Analyzing 91,608 articles covering 705 …

papers.title: The Emergence of Psychological Safety or its Mirage
papers.abstract: Leaders often strive to foster psychological safety in teams, and yet it may not emerge. This study builds grounded theory on how psychological safety emerges, or not, on teams. We draw on longitudinal ethnographic data from a matched pair case study of two teams over two years, including verbatim meeting transcripts that elicit the micro-processes affecting psychological safety and interviews that elucidate team members’ interpretations. We identify an illusion initially present on both teams in which surface markers of psychological safety existed but team members nonetheless continued to avoid interpersonal risk—what we call a psychological safety mirage. This occurred because external pressures on leaders spurred them to take self-protective actions that inadvertently reinforced interpersonal risk, despite their continued efforts to invite contributions. One team was eventually able to break from this mirage through a three-phase de-risking process that facilitated psychological safety emergence: (1) collectively recognizing the underlying risk faced by team members, (2) de-risking contributions by offering opportunities to build skills, through which safety was demonstrated and reinforced, and (3) enacting psychological safety, with all team members contributing, reinforcing, and sharing in the benefits of reduced interpersonal risk. This paper advances theory on psychological safety by conceptualizing a team-level de-risking process model that facilitates its emergence …

papers.title: How Firms Respond to Carbon Taxation
papers.abstract: Although environmental regulations can incentivize firms to reduce emissions, how firms adapt may depend not only on their organizational characteristics but also on the physical realities of their assets. This paper examines how multinational spread, an organizational feature in which firms own and manage similar production activities across countries, and the physical asset characteristics of production facilities jointly shape firms’ responses to carbon taxation. Using global, real-time satellite data on carbon emissions from 882 steel plants across 67 countries over 96 months (January 2015 to December 2022), we analyze operational adjustments firms can make to reduce carbon emissions: producing more cleanly by reducing emissions intensity of production or producing less by reducing asset utilization. We first examine how firms adapt to Canada’s carbon tax using a difference-in-differences (DID) design and then examine the impact of carbon taxes across countries using a stacked DID design. Our analysis reveals that, following Canada’s carbon tax, firms without multinational spread reduce carbon emissions primarily by lowering asset utilization; in contrast, firms with multinational spread additionally reduce emissions intensity of production. Importantly, our analysis of carbon taxes across countries shows that multinational spread alone does not dictate firm adaptation. Adaptation is fundamentally influenced by the physical technology on the ground: firms with …

papers.title: Effortful vs. Opportunistic Consumption of Discretionary Time: How Time-Reporting Decisions Influence Extra-Role Effort
papers.abstract: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities. Once employees have completed in-role tasks, discretionary time remains, which they may allocate to extra-role activities or consume opportunistically. This study examines how managers’ time-reporting decisions, as a less intrusive form of control, affect subordinates’ effort-allocation decisions. I propose two opposing predictions. First, managers’ control implementations may signal distrust, resulting in more opportunism and thus less extra-role effort. Second, I identify value signaling as a novel theoretical mechanism through which time-reporting decisions may increase extra-role effort. The main experiment manipulated two factors: the type of time report (aggregated versus disaggregated) and its implementation source (managerial choice versus random assignment) to isolate signaling effects from monitoring effects. Results reveal that when managers choose not to implement disaggregated time reporting—that is, reports that make discretionary time salient—subordinates significantly reduce their extra-role effort. Structural equation modeling shows that value signaling outweighs distrust signaling in driving employees’ effort-allocation decisions. In contrast, when the time-reporting format is randomly assigned, effort remains unchanged, underscoring the signaling role of managerial choice. An additional online experiment shows …

papers.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
papers.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with …

papers.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
papers.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .

papers.title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
papers.abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: K. J. Mitchener thanks the Ciocca Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Santa Clara University for funding this research (Grant 2024-CIOG11). Any views expressed in this paper exclusively represent those of the …

papers.title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
papers.abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04942 .

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Effect of State-Mandated Employment Certificates on Child Labor Violations in the United States
papers.abstract: The number of minors involved in child labor violations in the United States more than tripled from 2017 to 2025. Compounding this issue, several state legislatures have recently weakened child labor protection laws. A key component of these laws is whether employers are required to obtain an employment certificate when hiring minors under 18 years of age, which typically requires a parent’s signature and is issued by a school. Proponents of loosening child labor regulations argue that there is a lack of evidence demonstrating the effectiveness of these laws in reducing child labor violations. In this study, we examine the effect of state-mandated employment certificates on reducing child labor violations. We find that the requirement leads to an average of 13.3% fewer violation cases (not statistically significant), 31.8% fewer minors involved in child labor violations, and 34.9% lower civil penalties per minor, indicating reduced severity of violations that do occur. The negative effects on the number of cases and minors persist after addressing endogeneity concerns, as assessed using two novel instrumental variables. papers.title: Navigating Institutional Friction in Digital Transformation: A Mechanism‐Based View
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital transformation (DT) fundamentally alters organizational structures, practices, and values, frequently generating significant friction as incoming digital artefacts structurally misalign with legacy institutional demands. These demands are rooted in institutional logics—the deeply held belief systems and practices that guide organizational behaviour. Drawing on a 15‐year longitudinal case study of a Swedish municipality, this study investigates how public‐sector entities manage this friction over time. The findings reveal DT as a dynamic, recursive trajectory driven by three sociotechnical mechanisms: Consolidation, Control, and Negotiation. These mechanisms generate non‐linear shifts across institutional states of conflict and alignment. This study makes three contributions. First, it reconceptualizes DT theory by framing transformation as recursive, non‐linear cycles of divergence and convergence that redirect, suppress, or accommodate localized, logic‐based resistance. Second, it advances the logic multiplicity framework by demonstrating how digital artefacts alter sociotechnical coupling, thereby shifting the centrality and compatibility of competing demands. Third, it illuminates the causal architecture of macro‐level institutional change, detailing the observable actions used to navigate logic‐based resistance during DT.

papers.title: Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
papers.abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. papers.title: Uncertainty Attitudes, Subjective Beliefs, and Decisions Under Uncertainty
papers.abstract: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions. We collect data on (i) individual attitudes toward risk and ambiguity, including individual-specific probability weighting and loss aversion, and (ii) individual probabilistic beliefs about events related to the decisions we consider. The joint availability of individual preference parameters and subjective beliefs allows us to study heterogeneity and cross-correlations across these parameters in depth and to estimate structural models of decision making under uncertainty that go beyond subjective expected utility. We find that both preferences and beliefs are highly heterogeneous. Compared with subjective expected utility, prospect theory combined with source-dependent probability weighting fits the data strictly better in some contexts and equally well in others. Prospect theory performs particularly well when the belief distribution is concentrated toward extreme values. papers.title: Growth Paths in Early Machine Learning Ventures: Technical Configuration and Competitive Advantage Over Time
papers.abstract: Machine learning capabilities have become important strategic assets, yet little is known about how their technical characteristics affect the competitive advantage of the firms that build them. Through an inductive, multicase study tracking six early-stage machine learning ventures in an accelerator program, we explore how their phases of specialization and exploration may be constrained by properties of the underlying technology. Our findings show how training data, learning paradigms, and model outputs depend on one another and on the applications they serve, and how these relationships change over time. This interdependence shapes firms’ growth paths, alternately expanding or limiting the strategic options available to them. Characteristics that confer an early competitive advantage can constrain later growth. We discuss the implications for strategy research on competitive advantage and path dependence in machine learning ventures.

papers.title: Governance of Hybrid Fintech Ecosystem: An Examination Using the Generativity‐Control Paradigm
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Digital platforms are increasingly leveraged to address social challenges in the financial sector. However, the fintech sector, particularly in developing economies, is inherently hybrid, creating distinct governance challenges. This study examined the applicability of generativity‐control governance literature to managing dual motives, a federated structure, and a trust‐based value orientation in hybrid fintech ecosystems. Drawing on the digital platform ecosystem governance literature as the theoretical foundation and the concept of holons from information ecology theory as the analytical lens, the study analysed interview data from 41 respondents representing the regulator, ecosystem orchestrator, fintech startups, financial institutions, incubators, and media in the Indian fintech ecosystem. It employed deductive reflexive thematic analysis to analyse the interview data and used secondary data to corroborate the findings. Accordingly, this study conceptualised complementors as holons exhibiting part‐whole behaviour, offering a novel theoretical explanation of how they maintain the generativity‐control balance and address governance challenges to achieve both economic and social outcomes simultaneously in hybrid fintech ecosystems. papers.title: EXPRESS: Securing Supply Chains: Subsidies, Insurance, and Hybrid Incentives under Costly Verification
papers.abstract: The rising frequency of supply-chain disruptions—driven by physical shocks and cyber intrusions—underscores the need for coordinated action between governments and private firms. Firms may underinvest in security because they do not internalize the broader social losses generated by supply-chain disruptions. Public intervention is complicated, however, because firms privately know their baseline network security, choose unobservable preventive effort, and are subject to costly and imperfect verification. We develop a game-theoretic framework to compare three policy approaches: an ex-ante, audit-based subsidy; an ex-post, inspection-based insurance mechanism; and hybrid mechanisms that combine preventive support with contingent protection. Insurance performs better in lower-security environments, where incidents under shirking remain sufficiently likely for claims inspection and denied coverage to provide credible deterrence. Subsidies perform better in moderate-to-high-security environments, where pre-incident verification remains effective even as disruptions become less frequent. In regions where both instruments are feasible, we use an efficiency index—prevention per unit of agency cost—to identify the preferred mechanism. We then analyze two hybrid designs. Under delayed inspection, the government provides an up-front subsidy but conditions coverage on post-incident verification. papers.abstract: There is ongoing interest in understanding how capabilities are developed by various actors in platform ecosystems. While much of the existing research has focused on the capabilities of platform owners, we know relatively little about how complementors build the capabilities necessary for their participation in ecosystems. In this paper, we argue that some platform ecosystems involve outsourcing contractual relationships between platform owners, complementors, and clients. This introduces a distinct setting—platform-based outsourcing ecosystems—which invites insights from the IS outsourcing literature. Traditionally, the IS outsourcing literature has assumed that vendors develop capabilities primarily through experiential learning in dyadic and mediated settings, with evidence for learning between vendors in outsourcing ecosystems. Building on this foundation, we conducted a case study of a complementor operating on the AliCloud platform to examine how capability development unfolds in such ecosystems. Our analysis reveals a learning process shaped by changing contractual relationships: the complementor begins with vicarious learning under subcontracting from the platform owner, transitions to experiential learning under direct contracting with clients, and finally adopts reciprocal experiential learning as a sub-platform owner working with other complementors. In each phase, the complementor assumes a distinct role that reflects its contractual relationships with other …

papers.title: Overall Evaluation Criteria for A/B Tests: A Meta-Analytic Approach
papers.abstract: This paper discusses meta-analytic methods for estimating the value of marketing interventions given a database of historical A/B tests with multiple outcome variables.

papers.title: The role of algorithmic accountability in shaping developers’ deontological judgements and implementation behaviours
papers.abstract: Organisations increasingly delegate consequential judgements to algorithmic decision-making systems (ADMS)—software that renders decisions with minimal human intervention, as in credit scoring and fraud detection. Such systems can produce unethical outcomes that cause substantial reputational and societal harm, including discrimination against minorities. Prior research has mainly evaluated ethical outcomes after deployment, yet their foundations are laid earlier, during development. At this stage, developers must rely on deontological reasoning, evaluating design choices against moral imperatives such as fairness and non-discrimination, because actual consequences cannot yet be observed. In practice, deontological reasoning often falls short, as it is cognitively demanding and inconsistently motivated. Drawing on deontological ethics, we examine how perceived algorithmic accountability orients developers towards deontological judgements and behaviours, and the conditions under which this effect is amplified. Using a multi-method design comprising a survey (n = 148), an online experiment (n = 102), and qualitative interviews (n = 15) with ADMS developers, we find that developers perceiving higher algorithmic accountability engage more in deontological judgements and behaviours. These relationships strengthen with greater ADMS knowledge and within a deontological work climate. papers.title: Making agentic AI explainable and auditable
papers.abstract: Agentic AI promises operational speed, yet in finance, opaque decision paths hinder regulatory auditability. We address this autonomy paradox with a knowledge-enabled explainability (KEE) design theory that makes compliance an intrinsic, explicitly governed system property. KEE decouples probabilistic learning from an explicit, rule-governed reasoning layer, relocating epistemic uncertainty from opaque model inference to a semantic structure that can be inspected, contested, and updated. This enables ante-hoc structural control through a semantic, programmable graph that encodes regulatory mandates as executable, inspectable constraints. The theory specifies three design principles: structural knowledge codification, topological reasoning scaffolding, and adaptive synchronization. It also introduces six guidelines that operationalize regulator-acceptable, path-based audit trails. A longitudinal study of a multinational fintech platform provides naturalistic evidence that KEE can support high-velocity operations while producing path-based audit trails and accommodating controlled changes to regulatory logic. The study contributes to design science by theorizing auditable autonomy as ante-hoc structural control, specifying the entity-concept-event paradigm as its ontological mechanism, and formalizing this mechanism as a prescriptive design theory for regulated agentic AI.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Customer-to-Manufacturer: Should a Platform Cooperate with More Manufacturers?
papers.abstract: The traditional top-down relationship between manufacturers and consumers has led to persistently high failure rates in new product development. In response, the emerging customer-to-manufacturer (C2M) model leverages online platforms as intermediaries to directly transmit consumer feedback to manufacturers, thereby improving decision-making in product innovation and increasing the likelihood of product success. This paper develops an analytical model to study the strategic adoption of the C2M model in an online marketplace with one platform and two competing manufacturers. We focus on the role of platform information and examine how its trade-offs shape market outcomes. Our analysis shows that the impact of platform information on manufacturers' expected profits is non-monotonic. Moreover, manufacturers' cooperation decisions in C2M depend on the information price and are moderated by the amount of information. For the platform, unexpectedly, involving more manufacturers in C2M cooperation is not always optimal, especially when information is sufficient. We further show that the C2M model benefits the platform and consumers and improves social welfare, while potentially reducing manufacturers' profits. Overall, our results provide managerial and regulatory implications for platform-based C2M practices.

papers.title: Swap and Save: How a Button Shapes Lasting Online Grocery Shopping Behavior
papers.abstract: A well-documented phenomenon in the literature is that consumers exhibit persistence in their choices. Using data from the mineral water category on a price comparison platform that delivers real-time prompts of cheaper alternatives through "swap and save" buttons, this study examines whether and how these prompts influence persistent product choices in online grocery shopping. The findings reveal that shoppers who switched to an alternative product after receiving a prompt were 23.7 percentage points more likely to select that alternative product in subsequent visits, with this effect lasting for up to 10 shopping trips. Our analysis suggests that this sustained impact is driven not by long-term cost savings but by product discovery enabled through these real-time prompts.

papers.title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
papers.abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. papers.title: Injunctive Norms Outperform Reciprocity: Tip Request Messages Can Increase Tipping Without Reducing Demand
papers.abstract: Tip request messages are marketing communications that can help digital platforms balance customer spending with worker effort and compensation. We report the first field experiments manipulating tip request message content, analyzing 435,969 transactions. We test how three appeals based on tipping motivations–injunctive norms (“It’s customary to leave a tip for the seller’s service”), personalized reciprocity and impersonal reciprocity–affect tipping and future demand in a global freelance marketplace. On the web, first exposures to the injunctive norms message increased new buyers’ tipping rate by 11.8 percentage points (p.p.), and repeat buyers’ tipping rate by 6.8 p.p. In the app, first exposures to the injunctive norms message increased tipping rate by 2.5 p.p. for new buyers and 1.4 p.p. for repeat buyers. Treatment effects on tipping increase with transaction order price. The norms and personalized reciprocity messages increased subsequent orders and spending in the web experiment, and did not significantly change repatronage in the app experiment, suggesting that effective tipping prompts need not reduce future business. Overall, tip request messages can motivate customer tipping to better incentivize and compensate gig workers, but optimization requires careful testing.

papers.title: EXPRESS: The Role of Ease-of-Return Experience on Contingent Free Shipping Policies
papers.abstract: Contingent free shipping (CFS) policies, whereby consumers get free shipping if their orders exceed a certain amount, are commonplace. Such a policy aims to nudge customers to place larger orders by adding additional items and/or buying more expensive items ( order-swelling ). papers.title: EXPRESS: Revitalizing the Grocery Store Experience: An Empirical Study on the Spillover Effects of Experiential Services
papers.abstract: Grocery retailers increasingly use experiential services to attract customers to their stores. However, it remains unclear whether these services generate positive spillover effects to core grocery sales or cannibalize existing demand. papers.title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
papers.abstract: Data privacy regulations empower consumers to control the collection of their personal data. A significant consequence of these regulations is their effect on various data-driven business solutions, especially on personalization technologies and recommender systems. We investigate the potential impacts of diverse real-world data privacy practices (that can be adopted by firms in response to various data protection regulations) on the recommender systems performance. We also examine how these impacts vary across different personalization contexts and applications. In particular, we distinguish between scenarios where the user population exhibits more stable vs. more dynamic (i.e., changing) preferences, as these scenarios often represent distinctly different recommendation settings. We use a simulation framework, carefully seeded with real-world data, for a comprehensive evaluation of the recommender system performance under numerous scenarios, such as different recommendation algorithms, different data privacy practices, different degrees of users' preference dynamics, etc. Extensive computational experiments uncover several robust performance patterns for different data privacy practices and highlight substantial differences between recommendation settings with stable vs. changing user preferences. papers.title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
papers.abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. papers.title: Willingness to Compete in Dirty Competitions
papers.abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. papers.title: Inflexibility and Leverage
papers.abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. Higher inflexibility leads to lower financial leverage, potentially due to higher default risk and lower value of tax shields. Contraction inflexibility determines leverage more than expansion inflexibility. Moreover, our inflexibility measure explains financial leverage significantly better than other variables that potentially capture certain aspects of adjustment costs for capital or labor. In addition, inflexible firms increase leverage more following a positive credit supply shock. Analyses employing instrumental variables estimation confirm our main finding. Our results suggest inflexibility shapes corporate financial policies. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. papers.abstract: This paper frames the overlap violation problem in online advertising auctions as a missing-data problem and proposes a matrix completion approach to correct the resulting bias in observational studies with algorithmic ad allocation.

papers.title: Frontiers: Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure human preferences and opinions, but their outputs can diverge from human responses. We introduce human mimicry calibration (HuMCal), a post hoc, model-agnostic method that uses aggregate human benchmark data to learn how to combine LLM outputs from different prompts, personas, and model checkpoints. In applications to consumer transaction data and public opinion surveys, HuMCal improves agreement with human benchmarks over standard aggregation rules, and the calibrated weights often remain useful across time, geography, industry, and question clusters.

papers.title: EXPRESS: Coevolution of Trader Similarity Networks and Follower Dynamics in Social Trading
papers.abstract: Social trading platforms have been gaining popularity against traditional brokerages over the past few years. Compared with traders on traditional financial markets, those on social trading platforms often exhibit more similar trading strategies. In this paper, we examine the impact of strategy similarity patterns on traders' popularity. We identify two competing effects of similarity: a substitution effect, whereby traders with similar strategies become interchangeable and compete for followers; and a social proof effect, whereby similarity signals credibility in an environment characterized by high uncertainty and limited verifiable credentials, thereby attracting followers. To empirically examine these effects, we construct a dynamic similarity network and develop a coevolution model that captures the joint evolution of network structure and follower dynamics. Using data from a leading social trading platform, we find that, on average, greater similarity leads to a decline in a trader’s followers over time, indicating that the substitution effect dominates. Importantly, this relationship is heterogeneous. For more established traders, the substitution effect is stronger, such that greater similarity reduces their popularity. In contrast, for less established traders, the social proof effect dominates, and similarity increases their popularity. papers.abstract: Multi-entry betting pools for single-elimination tournaments create a portfolio-design problem: a participant may submit several brackets whose scores are highly dependent, while payouts are typically concentrated on the best-performing entry. Motivated by March Madness pools, we study the problem of selecting a portfolio of brackets that maximizes the expected maximum score (EMS) across entries. This objective captures the top-heavy nature of such contests without requiring a model of opponents' bracket choices, which is difficult to estimate reliably in a tournament played only once per year. We first establish computational and structural properties of the EMS objective. Exact EMS evaluation is #P-hard in general, although it is polynomial-time computable for any fixed number of entries with an exponent that grows with the portfolio size. For two entries, EMS decomposes into single-entry expected-score terms and an expected absolute score-gap term, making explicit the trade-off between selecting individually strong brackets and diversifying across outcomes. These insights motivate two sample average approximation algorithms: an entry-by-entry method based on marginal EMS contributions and a round-by-round method that exploits the geometrically increasing scoring weights in March Madness by emphasizing late-round diversification. papers.abstract: Online healthcare communities (OHCs) play an important role in transforming healthcare delivery. While existing literature has primarily focused on the impact of teleconsultation services on offline demand, the influence of integrating offline access into OHCs on teleconsultation remains largely unexplored. This study addresses the gap by investigating how the integration of offline access into OHCs affects the utilization of teleconsultation services. We leverage a natural experiment in an OHC involving the implementation of the Online Booking of Healthcare Appointments (OBHA) feature, which allows patients to secure in-person visit appointments in the OHC. Using difference-in-differences (DID) models, we find a significant increase in new demand for adopter physicians’ teleconsultation services following the integration of OBHA, without deterioration in service quality. Notably, the increased demand largely comes from patients in remote and underserved areas seeking consultations with high-quality physicians, exhibiting a cascading effect. Furthermore, we find that OBHA adoption extends the geographic reach of physicians’ teleconsultation services and promotes a more equitable distribution of teleconsultation utilization across regions. Our findings indicate that integrating offline access into OHCs not only boosts the utilization of teleconsultation services but also helps reduce health disparities by facilitating access to high-quality resources. papers.title: Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
papers.abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research.

papers.title: HOW AND WHY CHANGE AGENTS LEVERAGE AMBIGUITY: DIGITAL CHANGE AS A PROGRESSION OF PROCESS CONFIGURATIONS
papers.abstract: Digital change (DC) broadly entails a radical reconfiguration of an organization’s modus operandi through the deployment of a growing and often untried set of digital technologies. Prior research has extensively examined DC in terms of outcomes, antecedents, and mechanisms. However, one critical aspect remains underexplored: the role of ambiguity arising from unknown technologies, non-linear change processes, and the coexistence of multiple organizational goals. Existing DC literature commonly attributes failure to an inability to remove ambiguity – that is, the contested and fluid meanings, goals, and means of DC – and to align clear strategic intent with well-defined technology functions. We challenge this view by conceptualizing ambiguity not as a problem to be eliminated, but as an inherent and generative condition of DC that must be actively reckoned with. Drawing on March’s distinction between goal ambiguity and technology ambiguity, we develop a framework of four DC configurations based on the presence or absence of ambiguity in strategic intent and in the articulated role of digital technologies. We analyze four DC cases, treating each as a progression through shifting configurations of goal and technology ambiguity. Using three longitudinal empirical cases and one baseline alignment case from prior literature, we identify four distinct DC pathways, each characterized by a specific sequence of configurations. We theorize how ambiguity shapes DC trajectories and …

papers.title: Robust Auction Design with Support Information
papers.abstract: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of …

papers.title: From Employer Responsibility to Environmental Irresponsibility: Unintended Impacts of Social Insurance Law on Pollution Emissions
papers.abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. The mechanism analysis indicates that the enforcement of the law increases firms’ labor costs and financial distress, motivating them to reduce efforts on end-of-pipe treatment activities and measures taken during the production process, which results in higher pollution emission intensity. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Y. Li acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72403026]. Y. Qin acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72342031]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00714 .

papers.title: Estimating the Pricing Kernel: A Simple Regression-Based Dimension-Reduction Approach
papers.abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance.
